analysis.title: AI Crowding Out... And Back In
key_insights: Dario Perkins rejects the textbook 'crowding out' thesis that heavy AI capex funding demand mechanically pushes up government borrowing costs, calling it a fake loanable-funds model. The financial system flexes in response to new investment opportunities, and the cost of capital often falls during booms.

Three holes in the textbook thesis: no statistical relationship between security issuance and yields, many government bond buyers have mandates that bar them from risky tech securities, and AI-related debt trades at a discount to other corporate bonds with wider spreads.

A softer version holds that the AI boom is demand stimulus that raises inflation and forces the Fed to keep rates higher, damping rate-sensitive activity such as residential construction, durable goods and housing. Jason Furman is named as a proponent.

The AI buildout is net inflationary through higher energy costs and tech supply-chain bottlenecks, which lift both PPI and CPI. The effect on CPI is about 0.3 percentage points, with a larger effect on PPI.

Interest rates would probably be somewhat lower without the AI boom, but not by much. The macro footprint of the buildout is smaller than commonly assumed, and much of the US stimulus leaks abroad. Tech exports are adding about 20 percentage points to GDP in Korea and Taiwan.

The more important channel is perception of the monetary stance. The strong stock market made financial conditions look loose, and non-residential construction job gains have masked residential losses. This has convinced officials that r* (the neutral rate) is higher than previously thought.

The author expects the AI boom to end eventually, after which the Fed will cut rates aggressively. Because there is room for non-tech demand to 'crowd in', the downturn is expected to be relatively mild and unlike 2008/09.

macro_indicators.interpretation: The AI buildout adds modestly to inflation, so it explains only a small part of why the Fed holds rates higher. The PPI effect is larger.

macro_indicators.indicator: Tech exports contribution to GDP, Korea and Taiwan
macro_indicators.interpretation: Indicates that much of the US AI investment stimulus leaks to the rest of the world, which lowers the US investment multiplier.

macro_indicators.indicator: Fed policy rate path after AI boom ends
macro_indicators.interpretation: The author expects aggressive Fed easing once the AI boom ends, which would cushion the downturn.

risk_factors: Officials may misjudge the monetary stance, with a strong equity market and AI-supported non-residential construction leading them to believe r* is higher than it is.
The AI boom ending would trigger a downturn, though the author expects it to be relatively mild.

key_data_points.context: The impact on PPI is larger than on CPI.
key_data_points.anchor: the impact is around 0.3%pts on the CPI (more than that on the PPI)

key_data_points.metric: Tech exports contribution to GDP in Korea and Taiwan
key_data_points.context: Cited as evidence that US AI stimulus leaks to the rest of the world.
key_data_points.anchor: When you see tech exports suddenly adding 20%pts to GDP in Korea and Taiwan

tension_points.bull_case: AI investment does not mechanically lift yields. There is no statistical link between issuance and yields, government bond buyers cannot buy risky tech debt, and the financial system expands to fund new investment.
tension_points.bear_case: The AI boom adds to inflation and shifts perceptions of r*, which keeps the Fed tighter and damps rate-sensitive sectors such as housing.

theme_stances.key_argument: The AI boom raises inflation only modestly and mainly alters perceptions of the monetary stance, so crowding out is overblown but not unfounded.
theme_stances.evidence: the crowding out thesis, while overblown

theme_stances.key_argument: When the AI boom ends the Fed will cut aggressively, leaving scope to crowd in non-tech demand and making the downturn mild.
